{"id": "f35959da-6cd9-42cc-9740-c64ecadb229d", "role": "assistant", "block_type": "tool_summary", "content": [{"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": "tooluse_HW5XbGh0LUnuFhDD6lDWKm", "status": "success", "content": [{"text": "{\"content\":{\"result\":[{\"rank_order\":1,\"title\":\"Kubernetes Control Plane\",\"context\":\"### Overview\\n\\nTo protect itself from being overloaded during periods of increased requests, the API Server limits the number of inflight requests it can have outstanding at a given time. Once this limit is exceeded, the API Server will start rejecting requests and return a 429 HTTP response code for \\\"Too Many Requests\\\" back to clients. The server dropping requests and having clients try again later is preferable to having no server-side limits on the number of requests and overloading the control plane, which could result in degraded performance or unavailability.\\n\\nThe mechanism used by Kubernetes to configure how these inflights requests are divided among different request types is called API Priority and Fairness. The API Server configures the total number of inflight requests it can accept by summing together the values specified by the `--max-requests-inflight` and `--max-mutating-requests-inflight` flags. EKS uses the default values of 400 and 200 requests for these flags, allowing a total of 600 requests to be dispatched at a given time. However, as it scales the control-plane to larger sizes in response to increased utilization and workload churn, it correspondingly increases the inflight request quota all the way till 2000 (subject to change). APF specifies how these inflight request quota is further sub-divided among different request types. Note that EKS control planes are highly available with at least 2 API Servers registered to each cluster. This means the total number of inflight requests your cluster can handle is twice (or higher if horizontally scaled out further) the inflight quota set per kube-apiserver. This amounts to several thousands of requests/second on the largest EKS clusters.\\n\\nTwo kinds of Kubernetes objects, called PriorityLevelConfigurations and FlowSchemas, configure how the total number of requests is divided between different request types. These objects are maintained by the API Server automatically and EKS uses the default configuration of these objects for the given Kubernetes minor version. PriorityLevelConfigurations represent a fraction of the total number of allowed requests. For example, the workload-high PriorityLevelConfiguration is allocated 98 out of the total of 600 requests. The sum of requests allocated to all PriorityLevelConfigurations will equal 600 (or slightly above 600 because the API Server will round up if a given level is granted a fraction of a request). To check the PriorityLevelConfigurations in your cluster and the number of requests allocated to each, you can run the following command.\\n\\n*[truncated \u2014 additional content omitted]*\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/scale-control-plane.html\"},{\"rank_order\":2,\"title\":\"Troubleshooting Amazon EKS networking issues at scale in an Enterprise scenario\",\"context\":\"### Step 1: Investigate the Amazon EKS control plane\\n\\nFirst, we examined the control plane components, focusing on API throttling. We analyzed the [API Priority and Fairness (APF)](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/cluster-administration/flow-control/) to check if a high number of simultaneously starting Pods overloaded the API server. In our review of the Amazon EKS API server, we found no evidence of throttling. This indicated that the control plane didn't cause the issue. For more information, see [API Priority and Fairness](https://aws.github.io/aws-eks-best-practices/scalability/docs/control-plane/#api-priority-and-fairness) on the EKS Best Practices Guides. Also, the control plane scales automatically when metrics, such as the number of worker nodes and size of the etcd database, exceed the defined limits. For more information, see [Amazon EKS improves control plane scaling and update speed by up to 4x](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/containers/amazon-eks-control-plane-auto-scaling-enhancements-improve-speed-by-4x/)\",\"url\":\"https://repost.aws/articles/ARMvpWa7AYScyBBPRr6xkvXw/troubleshooting-amazon-eks-networking-issues-at-scale-in-an-enterprise-scenario\"},{\"rank_order\":3,\"title\":\"Amazon EKS introduces Provisioned Control Plane | Containers\",\"context\":\"## Delivering predictable and high performance at scale\\n\\nAmazon EKS Provisioned Control Plane gives you the ability to pre-allocate control plane capacity from a set of new scaling tiers, ensuring predictable and high performance for your most demanding workloads. By provisioning capacity ahead of time, your cluster handles instantaneous traffic bursts without the need for control plane scaling, which is crucial for serving traffic during high-demand events or sudden workload spikes. These new scaling tiers unlock significantly higher control plane performance and scalability required for emerging workload patterns like ultra scale AI training/inference, high performance computing, or large-scale data processing.\\n\\nProvisioned Control Plane allows you to choose from multiple control plane scaling tiers (XL, 2XL, 4XL) with each tier offering well defined performance on these Kubernetes attributes:\\n\\n* API request concurrency \u2013 the volume of requests processed by the Kubernetes API servers concurrently\\n* Pod scheduling rate \u2013 the throughput at which the Kubernetes default scheduler assigns pods to nodes\\n* Cluster database size \u2013 the storage space allocated to etcd, the database that holds the cluster state/metadata\\n\\nOnce you designate a scaling tier to your cluster, EKS ensures sufficient capacity is always available to the control plane to meet the attribute values for that tier. You also get comprehensive visibility into your tier utilization through granular metrics for each attribute, available through both the EKS Prometheus metrics endpoint and Amazon CloudWatch metrics vended to your account. As your workload demands evolve, you can switch between scaling tiers or go back to the standard control plane at any time. Provisioned Control Plane is an opt-in feature with tiered pricing based on your capacity selection. Visit the Amazon EKS pricing page to learn more.\\n\\n| Scaling Tier | Tier attributes | | | Price ($/hr) |\\n| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |\\n| API Request Concurrency (seats) | Pod Scheduling Rate (pods/sec) | Cluster Database Size (GB) |\\n| XL | 1700 | 167 | 16 | $1.65/hr |\\n| 2XL | 3400 | 283 | 16 | $3.40/hr |\\n| 4XL | 6800 | 400 | 16 | $6.90/hr |\\n\\nTier attribute values are specific to the EKS cluster version. The above values apply to EKS version 1.30 and later. You can lookup the values for each version under our user guide. If you need higher attributes for your cluster beyond\\n\\n*[truncated \u2014 additional content omitted]*\",\"url\":\"https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/containers/amazon-eks-introduces-provisioned-control-plane/\"}]}}"}]}], "label": "Look up AWS docs on EKS API Priority and Fairness 429 responses"}

{"id": "b6b7467f-a39f-44df-8670-6cbca5edf2e4", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "A quick flag first: I don't have a specific "grading skill" loaded for EKS reviews, so I can't cite guard criteria from one. What I *can* do is walk through what AWS's own guidance says needs to be checked before this evidence can be called "API saturation" — which lines up with how a rigorous review would guard against a false positive here.

**What needs verifying before calling this "API saturation":**

1. **Which priority level, specifically.** `workload-low` is one of several `PriorityLevelConfigurations` (`system`, `leader-election`, `workload-high`, `workload-low`, `global-default`, etc.), each carved out of the *same* fixed inflight-request pool (600 by default, scaling up to 2000 as EKS auto-scales the control plane). A burst of 429s isolated to `workload-low` means that slice ran out of its allotted seats — it does **not** mean the API server as a whole was overloaded. You need to check whether `workload-high`, `leader-election`, and `system` were clean during the same window. If they were, this is APF doing its job of protecting higher-priority traffic, not the control plane failing.

2. **Correlate with the deployment rollout mechanics, not just the timestamp.** A 3-minute burst coinciding with a rollout is classic signature of a client-side request storm — e.g., a Deployment/DaemonSet update triggering many simultaneous LIST/WATCH or PATCH calls from controllers, `kubectl rollout` polling, or a misbehaving controller retrying aggressively — all typically bucketed into `workload-low` by default FlowSchemas. Confirm what client/user-agent generated the rejected requests (`apiserver_flowcontrol_rejected_requests_total` by `flowSchema`, or audit logs) before assuming it's a capacity problem versus a client behavior problem.

3. **Check whether the control plane already auto-scaled.** EKS scales inflight quota automatically based on node count, etcd size, and workload churn. Check whether utilization metrics (`apiserver_flowcontrol_request_concurrency_limit`, `apiserver_current_inflight_requests`) show the control plane was already at an elevated tier and still saturated at `workload-low`, versus running at a baseline tier where the burst was simply absorbed by design.

4. **Duration and recurrence.** A one-off 3-minute burst tied to a specific rollout event is very different from a sustained or recurring pattern. Guards against overreacting to isolated bursts are usually looking for repeat occurrences or bursts unrelated to any specific event.

**Does this justify scaling the control plane?**

Not on this evidence alone. AWS's own troubleshooting pattern (see the EKS networking-at-scale writeup) explicitly treats APF rejections as something to *rule out* as a control-plane cause, not confirm it — they only treat it as control-plane saturation if higher-priority levels were also affected or global inflight limits were being hit. A `workload-low`-only, 3-minute, rollout-correlated 429 burst most plausibly indicates fair-scheduling working as intended against a bursty client — the fix is more likely to be on the client side (backoff/jitter in whatever triggered the rollout's API calls, or reducing rollout parallelism) or, if truly needed, adjusting FlowSchema/PriorityLevel concurrency shares — not scaling the control plane itself.

Want me to check your cluster's actual APF metrics (rejected requests by priority level, concurrency limits) for that window to confirm which of these it is?", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
